items.new: Wet and drenched through, shivering with cold, having given up hope of either ship or boat, we raised our eyes as dawn broke. The mist still lay spread over the sea, and the empty lantern lay crushed in the bottom of the boat. Suddenly Queequeg leaped to his feet and cupped his hand to his ear. We all heard a faint creaking, like the sound of ropes and yards that the storm had muffled until now. It came closer and closer; a huge, vague shape dimly parted the thick mist. In terror we all jumped into the sea as the ship finally loomed into view, bearing straight down on us, hardly more than her own length away.

items.new: There is one more small point about gamming that must not be forgotten here. Every profession has its own little peculiarities of detail, and so does the whale fishery. On a pirate ship, a man-of-war, or a slave ship, when the captain is rowed anywhere in his boat, he always sits in the stern sheets on a comfortable seat, sometimes a cushioned one, and often does his own steering with a pretty little milliner's tiller trimmed with bright cords and ribbons. But the whale-boat has no seat in the stern, no sofa of any kind, and no tiller at all. It would be a fine state of affairs indeed if whaling captains were wheeled over the water on casters, like gouty old aldermen in patent chairs. As for a tiller, the whale-boat never stands for any such effeminacy. So, since a whole boat's crew must leave the ship when gamming, and since the boat-steerer, or harpooner, is one of them, that subordinate does the steering on these occasions, and the captain, with nowhere to sit, is rowed off to his visit standing straight up like a pine tree. You will often notice that this standing captain, aware that the eyes of the whole visible world are fixed on him from the sides of both ships, is keenly conscious of how important it is to keep his dignity by keeping his feet. That is no easy matter. Behind him the huge projecting steering oar knocks him now and then in the small of the back, and in front the after-oar returns the compliment by rapping his knees. So he is wedged in completely, front and back, and can only widen himself sideways by settling down on his spread legs; but a sudden, violent pitch of the boat will often come close to toppling him, because a long foundation is worthless without a matching breadth. Just set two poles in a spread angle, and you will not be able to stand them up. Then again, it would never do — never, I say — for this straddling captain to be seen, in plain view of the world's riveted eyes, steadying himself the least bit by grabbing anything with his hands. In fact, to show his complete, buoyant self-command, he usually keeps his hands in his trouser pockets; though perhaps, since they are usually very large, heavy hands, he keeps them there as ballast. Still, there have been cases, and well-documented ones too, where a captain has been known, for an unusually critical moment or two — in a sudden squall, say — to grab the nearest oarsman's hair and hang on like grim death.

items.new: "On the fourth day of sailing, they spotted a large canoe that seemed to have put in at a low coral island. The captain steered away from it, but the savage craft came bearing down on him, and soon Steelkilt's voice hailed him, ordering him to heave to or be run under water. He leveled a pistol. Standing with one foot on each prow of the lashed-together war-canoes, the Lakeman laughed him to scorn, and told him that if the pistol so much as clicked in its lock, he would bury him in bubbles and foam."

items.new: Whatever superstitions sperm whalemen in general have attached to the sight of this object, one thing is certain: because a glimpse of it is so very rare, that fact alone has done much to give it an air of ill omen. It is seen so seldom that, although every one of them declares it the largest living thing in the ocean, very few have more than the haziest notions of its real nature and shape. Even so, they believe it provides the sperm whale with his only food. Other kinds of whales find their food above water, where men can watch them eating; but the spermaceti whale gets all his food in unknown zones below the surface, and what exactly it consists of can only be worked out by inference. Sometimes, when hard pressed, he will throw up what are thought to be the detached arms of the squid, some of them more than twenty, even thirty, feet long. The whalemen imagine that the monster these arms belonged to usually clings by them to the ocean floor, and that the sperm whale, unlike other species, has teeth so that he can attack it and tear it apart.
